draft.title: Evaluative language
card: Evaluative language is made up of words that judge something as good or bad, right or wrong, or worth or not worth our time. Brilliant, careless and unfair are examples.
These words show the writer's opinion. Compare "The team lost the match" with "The team played a careless match". The first reports a fact. The second judges it.
Some judging words are stronger than others. Decent is mild, good is stronger, and outstanding is very strong. A writer picks the strength to match how strongly they feel.
Evaluative words also shape how a reader feels. Calling a rule unfair makes a reader likely to side against it.
draft.remember: Evaluative words judge, and the strength of the word shows how strongly the writer feels.

opts: The new library is a wonderful place to study
The new library opened on Monday morning
The new library has two floors and a café
The new library is on the corner of Park Street
a.why: Wonderful judges the library as good, so it shows the writer's opinion. The other sentences only give facts that can be checked, such as when it opened and where it is.
a.clue: Look for the word that says the library is good or bad.

b.q: Zoe wrote a review of a school play. Which word would show the strongest positive opinion if she put it in the blank: "The play was ___"?
opts: Spectacular
Pleasant
Acceptable
Long
b.why: Spectacular is a very strong word of praise. Pleasant and acceptable also judge the play, but they are mild. Long is tempting because it describes the play, but it is a fact about length, not a strong opinion.
b.clue: Rank the three judging words from mild to strong, and ignore the one that is only a fact.

a.best: The new library is a wonderful place to study

problems.detail: The clue and the why call 'long' only a fact. 'The play was long' is relative and often carries a negative judgement (too long or dull), so it is not purely a checkable fact. This could confuse students about what counts as evaluative. The right answer is not affected.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The only issue is that question b's clue and why treat 'long' as purely factual, when it can carry a negative judgement.
